lessonRef.focus: ordering grouped reasons and linking them to the opinion
lessonRef.title: Guided practice B: ordering grouped reasons and linking them to the opinion

studentTask.text: This Grade 4 lesson develops ordering grouped reasons and linking them to the opinion within the unit “Opinion and Argument: Reasons, Evidence, and Fair Reading.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's guided practice b work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
When a growing city decides how to move people, it usually chooses among three approaches. Each one solves a real problem and creates a different one.

The first approach is to widen roads. This is the most popular choice, because the benefit appears immediately: more lanes carry more cars, and a commute that took thirty-five minutes may take twenty-five. The difficulty is a pattern transportation planners call induced demand. When driving becomes easier, more people choose to drive, and some who had moved closer to work move farther away. Studies of American metropolitan areas have repeatedly found that within about five to ten years, traffic volume rises roughly in proportion to the new lane capacity, and travel times return close to where they began.

The second approach is to build rail. A single light-rail line can carry far more people per hour than a lane of traffic, and it does so without adding vehicles to the street. The obstacle is cost and time. Rail requires purchasing land, relocating utilities, and years of construction before a single rider is served. A city facing congestion this year may be unwilling to spend heavily on a benefit that arrives in a decade, even when the arithmetic favors it.

The third approach is to improve buses. Buses use roads that already exist, so the cost is dramatically lower and service can begin within months. Giving buses a dedicated lane and signal priority produces much of the capacity benefit of rail at a fraction of the price. The obstacle here is political rather than technical: a dedicated bus lane takes a lane away from cars, and drivers can see exactly what they have lost while the benefit is spread across riders they never meet.

Notice that only one of these three obstacles is an engineering problem. The second is a budgeting problem, and the third is a problem of who is willing to give something up. A city that treats all three as engineering questions will keep widening roads and keep wondering why the traffic returns.

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “Three Ways to Move a City”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what ordering grouped reasons and linking them to the opinion asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “Three Ways to Move a City,” then answer: Identify one earlier misunderstanding about ordering grouped reasons and linking them to the opinion. Use this reading to correct it and explain why the correction is stronger.

Deliverable: Grade 4: a before-and-after correction supported by the source; write one organized paragraph.

Evidence requirement: Use two exact details. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If ordering grouped reasons and linking them to the opinion is not yet secure, return to “Three Ways to Move a City” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply ordering grouped reasons and linking them to the opinion to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “Three Ways to Move a City.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
